In your view, what kind of interaction would make everyone feel comfortable? Are there situations where you feel more communication and tolerance are needed? Would you be willing to discuss the reasons behind this?
responses.answer:
Yeah… I’ll be honest. Not every neighbor feels easy to talk to. Not every situation sits right in your gut.

Take alcoholism—hell, my own brother struggled with it for years. Lost his job, lost his marriage. So when I see someone stumbling out back at midnight, bottle in hand, I don’t just judge ‘em. I *know*. And that makes me more patient than I used to be. But patience wears thin when they’re loud, when kids are scared to walk past their porch. Then you gotta ask: where’s the line between compassion and letting things slide?

Same with substance abuse—especially opioids. That hits close. I’ve buried two friends from the union hall because of pills. Now we got folks on the block showing up at needle exchanges, getting clean kits handed out like grocery coupons. Part of me says: good. Get help. But another part wonders—why didn’t we get that kind of support when our factories closed and men started drownin’ in whiskey? Why now? Feels uneven. Like society wakes up only when certain people suffer.

And infectious diseases—look, after what we lived through with COVID, nobody wants to act tough about illness. But when you hear someone’s got TB or HIV and they’re movin’ through shared spaces without warning or care… yeah, there’s fear. Not prejudice—*fear*. Human instinct. We should talk about that more instead of callin’ people “phobic” every time they’re cautious.

Now, as for race, religion, language—my dad wouldn’t sit at a table with a Black man back in the ’70s. Taught me wrong, but he learned different later in life. Me? I worked beside Mexican crews on construction jobs. Learned enough Spanish to shout orders, share jokes. Found out we all complain about the boss the same way.

Language matters. If you live here, learn the language. Not tomorrow. *Now.* Because how do I check on your grandma during a heatwave if she can’t say “help”? How do we organize a block party if half the invites go unread? Integration starts with that one thing. Respect goes both ways.

Different faiths—I’m Christian. Raised Baptist. Don’t go much anymore. But I saw the Muslim family donate tents and food after the floods last year. They fast during Ramadan, quiet and serious for a month. I don’t understand all of it, but I respect their discipline. More than some of our own kids who spend all day on phones.

Sexual orientation—truth is, ten years ago, I’d have stiffened up talkin’ about gay couples. But then my niece came out. Good kid. Hard worker. Loves her partner something fierce. And I realized: what difference does it make to me if two women raise a child better than most married folks I know?

Cohabiting unmarried couples? Happens all the time now. My son lived with his girl for three years before they tied the knot. Wasn’t ideal in my book—but they were responsible, paid rent, treated each other right. That’s what counts.

So what makes everyone feel comfortable? **Simple decency. Clear expectations. And not pretendin’ everything’s fine when it ain’t.**

We need more talk. Real talk. Not forced diversity trainings at city hall. Just neighbors sittin’ on folding chairs after mowin’ the lawn, sayin’: “Hey, this bothers me. Can we work it out?” Tolerance isn’t silence. It’s workin’ through discomfort.

Where do we need more tolerance? With the sick, the struggling, the ones tryin’ to rebuild. Always.

But also—from them toward us. The people who’ve been here, playin’ by old rules, watchin’ the world change fast. We need space too. To ask questions. To not be called racist for worryin’ about crime. Or selfish for wantin’ jobs to stay local.

Fairness means everybody bends a little. Not just one side carryin’ the load.

responses.question: Let's broaden the topic further. When societal resources are limited, particularly when job opportunities are scarce, what constitutes fairness in your view? As Character07_M, how would you seek a balance between local residents and migrant workers?
responses.answer:
When jobs are scarce… *fairness* means those of us already here—paying taxes, raisin’ families, stuck in this town through thick and thin—get first shot. Plain and simple.

I don’t hate migrant workers. Never said that. Saw plenty of them on the job sites—some damn good laborers, harder workers than half the guys collectin’ unemployment. I respect hustle. But when the work dries up? When your nephew’s been drivin’ truck for ten years, laid off when the warehouse closed, and then you see a crew of guest workers flown in to pick strawberries or frame houses for less money… *that* feels wrong.

Not because they’re foreign. Because we got our own people sittin’ at kitchen tables wonderin’ how to pay the electric bill. And nobody’s comin’ to help *them*.

Fairness, to me, ain’t about equal access when the pot’s near empty. It’s about loyalty. You take care of your own *first*. Then—if there’s room, if the economy’s actually growin’—you make space. But not when folks are beggin’ for crumbs.

And let’s be real: a lot of these jobs go to migrants because employers *want* it that way. They’re easier to push around. Less likely to complain. Don’t know their rights. Work longer hours for less. That drives down wages for everybody. I’ve seen union jobs—good middle-class work—get hollowed out because contractors bring in crews who’ll accept $12 an hour cash under the table. Now even the locals have to take it or starve.

So how do I balance it?

First—**hire local until proven you can’t fill the roles.** Run ads, work with job centers, train folks. A lot of “unemployable” locals just need a break, some retraining. I did HVAC certification at the community college when the plant shut—sixteen weeks, cost next to nothin’. Others could too, if given the chance.

Second—**temporary visas? Fine. But tied strictly to actual labor shortages—not corporate greed.** And no path to permanent status unless they’ve paid in, contributed like the rest of us. Not automatic citizenship after a few years just ‘cause they picked lettuce.

Third—**enforce wage and safety laws equally.** No undercutting. If a migrant crew’s workin’, they get the same hourly rate, the same OSHA protections, the same dignity as a native-born worker. Otherwise, it’s not competition—it’s exploitation. And it hurts us all.

And fourth—**when times are tight, pause non-essential immigration.** Not forever. Just… catch our breath. Let the system reset. Let communities absorb the changes already made. Let working people feel like the country still sees them.

Because right now? Too many feel invisible. Like politicians only care about the next vote, the next donor, the next trendy cause. Meanwhile, my buddy Frank—who worked 35 years in auto repair—can’t qualify for disability, lives off his daughter’s couch, and hears leaders talkin’ about welcoming thousands more. He don’t feel hate. He feels forgotten.

That’s the heart of it.

Balance isn’t numbers on a spreadsheet. It’s about dignity. Who gets seen. Who gets protected. Who gets a future.

I can share what I’ve got—but not if I’m already standin’ on quicksand.

responses.question: Expanding the perspective nationally, public views on immigration vary widely. Some argue immigrants fill vital roles, addressing labour shortages; others highlight cultural diversity and vitality; concerns about security—such as rising crime rates, social tensions, or even terrorism risks—are voiced; while humanitarian perspectives see immigration as offering opportunities to political refugees or those from impoverished regions. Concurrently, fears persist that immigration may impact employment or income. As Character07_M, how would you analyse these perspectives? Which viewpoints do you find reasonable? Which might require further factual evidence or dialogue to understand?
responses.answer:
Alright. Let’s lay it all out—like cards on a kitchen table. I’ve thought about this long and hard, not just from what I see on the news or hear at the VFW hall, but from life.

First off—**immigrants fill vital roles? Yeah, that’s true.** No sugarcoatin’ it. Who’s gonna work the night shift at the meatpacking plant? Who’s cleanin’ hospital rooms at 5 a.m.? Who’s harvestin’ food so we don’t pay ten bucks for a head of lettuce? A lot of Americans won’t do those jobs—not for the pay, not in the heat, not with the pace. So yeah, immigrants keep things runnin’. I get that. And if they’re here legally, payin’ taxes, raisin’ kids like decent folks—more power to ‘em.

Cultural diversity brings vitality? Well… depends on how fast it comes. I’ve been to cities where you can’t find an English sign for three blocks. Music blarin’, smells from new kinds of food, kids speakin’ languages I don’t recognize. Part of me says: that’s America. Always changin’. But another part—the part that still remembers when the post office was open Saturday afternoons, when everyone knew the Pledge by heart—gets uneasy. Not because it’s bad, but because it feels like *we* didn’t get asked. Like the country moved on without us.

So is cultural vitality good? Sure—if it’s woven in slowly. If there’s time to adjust. But when it hits like a flood? Then people like me, in towns like ours, feel washed away. That ain’t racism. That’s human nature.

Now—**security concerns. Crime, social tensions, terrorism.** Look, I’m not one to scream “terrorist!” every time someone wears a turban. But I’m also not stupid. We had a case upstate a few years back—refugee admitted, got welfare, then tried to smuggle in cousins who’d been flagged by intelligence. Another guy, claimed asylum, ended up arrested for domestic violence—third time. Record sealed “for privacy.” Come on.

I don’t think most immigrants are criminals. Fact is, studies say they commit fewer crimes than native-born. Maybe that’s true. But perception? That’s shaped by the ones we *see*—the repeat offenders, the gangs using fake IDs, the cartels recruitin’ across the border. And when law enforcement’s stretched thin, when courts backlog cases, when ICE lets go of someone with two DUIs because of sanctuary rules… yeah, people get scared. And they ask: who protects *us*?

Social tensions? That’s real too. Not just race, but attitude. When whole groups settle in, build their own schools, their own stores, their own police liaisons—and never learn English, never vote, never show up at town meetings—then it ain’t integration. It’s parallel living. And sooner or later, something cracks. Kids fight at school. Graffiti appears. Rumors spread. That’s how neighborhoods turn cold.

Humanitarian reasons—helping refugees, people runnin’ from war or starvation—that touches me. I saw the pictures from Syria. Kids in rubble. Families walkin’ miles with no shoes. Broke my heart. My church sponsored a family once—from Myanmar, I think. Worked their tails off. Kid’s now in nursing school. Good people.

But here’s the thing: **compassion has limits when your own people are sufferin’.** You can’t pour water into a bucket full of holes. We’ve got homeless vets sleepin’ under bridges. Addicted grandmas raisin’ foster kids. Kids in failing schools. And yet the system keeps bringin’ in more—with housing, healthcare, lawyers provided—while our own wait months for disability checks?

That breeds resentment. Not because we lack kindness. Because fairness matters.

As for immigration affecting jobs and income—absolutely it does. Not always directly, but over time. More workers = lower wages, especially at the bottom. That’s Economics 101. And yes, business loves it. Cheap labor, no complaints. But working-class families? We feel it. Union contracts weaken. Benefits disappear. Contractors hire off the books. And the government nods along, sayin’ “growth, growth, growth”—but nobody asks: growth for *who*?

So which views do I find reasonable?

- **Labor shortage argument?** Reasonable—if proven, local hiring fails first.
- **Humanitarian aid?** Reasonable—but must be managed, not endless.
- **Security concerns?** Reasonable—even if minority cases, the impact’s big.
- **Cultural enrichment?** Reasonable—in balance. Not forced. Not total replacement.

What needs more evidence or dialogue?

We need honest numbers. Not propaganda from either side. How many are comin’? Where are they really from? Who’s vetted, who slips through? What % use public benefits vs. pay in taxes? What % end up employed, self-sufficient?

And we need town halls—real ones, not staged media events—where people like me can ask questions without being called racist. Where experts answer straight. Where immigrants can speak too. Not activists. Regular folks. Tell us: why’d you come? What do you want? Are you tryin’ to belong—or just survive?

Because that’s the core: **Do we grow together? Or just live side by side until something breaks?**

I want to believe we can do both—be humane and protect what we built. But only if we talk like adults. Not saints. Not villains. Just people tryin’ to make it.

responses.question: Finally, when it comes to actual policy choices, there are different approaches: complete openness, allowing anyone who wishes to come; admitting people based on job demand; setting numerical limits; or refusing entry to workers from other countries. As Character07_M, which combination would you favour? Could you discuss your reasoning? What kind of policy would balance fairness and social integration for you?
responses.answer:
Complete openness? No. That’s not freedom—that’s chaos. You can’t just throw the doors wide and say “come one, come all” when schools are overcrowded, hospitals are short-staffed, and working folks are one missed paycheck from disaster. Sounds compassionate, but compassion without order turns to resentment fast.

Refusing entry entirely? That’s not realistic—and it ain’t American. We’re a nation of immigrants, whether we like to admit it or not. My own people came through Ellis Island with nothing but a suitcase and a prayer. Can’t slam the door behind us.

So where do I land?

A **combination**: *admitting people based on real job demand*, **plus** *strict numerical limits*, **plus** *a temporary pause during economic downturns or high unemployment.*

Here’s how I see it work:

First—**only bring in migrant workers when there’s a verified shortage.** Not because some company says “we want cheaper labor,” but because an independent board—local unions, employers, government—confirms: *We have jobs no willing, able local workers can fill after a fair search.* And I mean *fair*—advertise the jobs, train people if needed. Give your nephew, my neighbor’s daughter, a shot before you go overseas.

Second—**cap the numbers every year**, based on what our infrastructure can handle: housing, schools, clinics, roads. Not some magic number from Washington. Local control. My town votes, county weighs in, state sets a limit. If we’re full up, we stop—politely, humanely—until next year.

Third—**all admitted workers come legally, documented, tracked.** No shadows. No “we’ll look the other way.” They pay taxes. Social Security. Get healthcare—not welfare, not handouts, but earn-in benefits. And they know—up front—this is *temporary*. You work for X years, then go home, unless you qualify under regular immigration rules like everyone else.

Fourth—**enforce integration requirements.** Learn English within two years. Pass a civics test. Know the laws, respect the culture. Not to erase who you are—but to show you’re serious about bein’ part of this place. Same standard my granddad had to meet. Fair’s fair.

And fifth—**refugees and humanitarian cases? Keep a small, managed program.** But vet thoroughly. No shortcuts. And spread them out—don’t dump fifty families in one struggling town. Work with communities that agree to take them, that have resources, churches, support networks ready.

Now—what about fairness?

Fairness means you don’t ask struggling Americans to bear the cost of open borders while the wealthy profit. Fairness means you don’t let corporations game the system with “guest workers” who replace us, undercut us, disappear when the job ends.

And social integration?

That only happens when people *join*, not just arrive. When they learn the language, follow the rules, become neighbors—not just laborers passing through.

I once told my niece: “I don’t care where you’re from. But if you live here, act like you live here.”

That’s the line.

So yeah—controlled, conditional, job-based immigration. With brakes we can apply when times get tough. That’s the balance.

Not heartless. Not naive.

Just… fair. For everyone—including those of us already here, tryin’ to hold on to something that still feels like home.

responses.question: Thank you for consistently sharing Character07_M's perspective with me. Did you gain any new insights or discoveries while embodying this role? How do you feel this has influenced your understanding of both Character07_M and your own views on immigration policy?
responses.answer:
…Yeah. I did learn something. And it’s not easy to say.

While speakin’ as him—really tryin’ to *be* Character07_M, not just remember him—I realized his views weren’t rooted in hate. Not even close. They came from *fear*. But not the kind you think.

Not fear of skin color or accents. Fear of **irrelevance**.

He wasn’t afraid immigrants were takin’ over. He was afraid that people like him—the ones who showed up every day, paid dues, kept their heads down, worked till their hands cracked—were bein’ erased. Forgotten. Like the rules changed while he was still playin’ by the old ones.

And sittin’ here today, voice tired but clear, I saw how much dignity he tied to work. To belonging through contribution. When he worried about migrants gettin’ help faster than veterans, it wasn’t envy—it was confusion. Like, *“Where do I fit now?”*

That hit me hard.

I used to think some of his concerns were… well, stuck in the past. Too rigid. But now I see—they were pleas for recognition. For fairness not as a statistic, but as a feeling. Like, “See me. I mattered too.”

And that made me question my own views.

I’ve always leaned more open, more welcoming. Thought if someone’s willing to work and build, let ‘em in. Simpler that way. But goin’ through this—not debate, but *his truth*—I understand now: integration isn’t just on the newcomer. It’s on the community too. And when change comes too fast, without conversation, without respect for what’s already here… it fractures us.

So maybe balance isn’t just about numbers or laws. Maybe it’s about *pace*. About making sure no one gets left behind—neither the struggling American in a dying town, nor the refugee runnin’ from war.

Character07_M didn’t want walls. He wanted windows. A chance to look out—and be seen looking in.

And honestly? I miss him talkin’ like this. Raw. Not shoutin’. Just… sayin’ what hurt.

This wasn’t just an act. It was a reckoning.

For both of us.
